title: Cracking the 2 x 2 options: right verdict and the reason that fits
blurb: Split every 'and why?' question into a verdict and a reason, and pick the one pair that is both right and relevant.
question: Four options: two say 'Yes, because...' and two say 'No, because...'. Every reason sounds like something from the manual. How do you find the single right answer?

teach.h: Two decisions hidden in one question
teach.body: Most classic Practitioner questions end 'and why?'. The four options form a 2 x 2 grid: two verdicts (yes or no, applies it well or poorly) crossed with two different reasons each. Exactly one verdict-and-reason pair is right. So every question is really two decisions: first the verdict, which removes half the options, then the reason, which must be both correct and the one that explains this situation.

teach.caption: Options A and B share a verdict, as do C and D. Get the verdict right and you are choosing between two.

teach.h: Five steps for every 'and why?' item

steps.label: Read the situation
steps.sub: Process, stage, who acted, what they did

steps.label: Name the test
steps.sub: The principle, practice or activity in quotes

teach.h: The verdict comes from the facts
teach.body: Decide the verdict by comparing what happened with the method: the activity's recommended actions, the RACI, the role rules and the principle's intent. Use the scenario facts, such as the delivery approach, the fixed date or the team's experience. Then test each remaining reason with 'this is right because...'. The winning reason names the rule the action follows or breaks, and it links to something in the stem.

Fernhollow Foods (scenario S4) is launching six chilled ready meals. At the end of the concept stage, consumer panel scores for two recipes are poor. Project manager Nadia Osei updates the business case to compare a four-recipe launch with six, and the board checks it is still worth continuing before authorizing development. How well does this apply 'ensure continued business justification'? Well: justification must stay valid and be revalidated throughout, and the board checks it at every stage end.

teach.h: The four options for the Fernhollow example

rows.label: B
values: Well: benefits are confirmed after closure

rows.label: C
values: Poorly: the executive should update it

rows.label: D
values: Poorly: a fixed launch date fixes the case

teach.caption: B is the dangerous one: a true statement about the business case that does not explain the board's check.

teach.h: Business case: signs of good and poor application
head: Applied well
Applied poorly
rows: Outline case before initiation, full case in initiation
No business case because the idea is 'obviously' right
PM updates the case at each stage end with actuals
Case frozen once the project is authorized
Board checks it at stage ends and exception plans
Board approves the next stage without checking it
Compulsory work still justifies the chosen option
'It is required by law, so no case is needed'
Benefits are measurable improvements from outcomes
teach.caption: Sources: PRINCE2 7 manual 2.1, 5.2 and 5.3.1.

teach.h: Why a wrong option is wrong
teach.caption: Examiners also swap in a neighbouring principle with a plausible reason.

teach.text: Two business case traps sit behind many 2 x 2 items. Continued business justification applies to compulsory projects too: the chosen option must still be justified as best value. And outputs, outcomes and benefits differ: a range of six ready meals is an output; shoppers buying the brand is an outcome; £6 million of branded sales a year is a benefit.

items: Four options = two verdicts x two reasons; one pair is right.
Decide the verdict from the scenario facts before reading the options.
The right reason is true in the method AND explains this situation.
Justification is checked at every stage end and when assessing an exception plan.
Compulsory work still needs its chosen option justified.

summary: You can now split an 'and why?' question into a verdict and a reason, use the scenario facts to decide the verdict, and reject reasons that are false or do not fit. You can also judge how well the S4 project applies continued business justification and the business case practice.

A.q: Fernhollow Foods' managing director has issued a mandate to launch the Fernhollow Kitchen range. During starting up, she tells the project manager that a business case is unnecessary, because the board has already decided that building its own brand is the right strategy. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
options: Well, because the mandate already explains why the project is needed
Well, because the detailed business case is prepared later, in initiation
Poorly, because an outline case is needed before initiation is authorized
Poorly, because the business case should be approved by the supermarket
A.why: There must be a justifiable reason to start, documented as the outline business case in starting up and checked by the board when it authorizes initiation (2.1, 5.3.1).

whyNot.0: The mandate triggers starting up; the outline business case is still developed from it.
whyNot.1: True that the full case is prepared in initiation, but an outline case is still needed first.
whyNot.3: The business case belongs to Fernhollow; the executive is accountable for it, not a customer.

A.q: Fernhollow Foods is at the end of the development stage of the Fernhollow Kitchen launch. The project manager updates the business case with actual costs to date, the revised cost of the new line and the latest sales forecasts, and the board reviews it before authorizing the trials stage. How well does this apply the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Well, because the case is updated at stage ends with actuals and forecasts
Well, because the benefits are confirmed by reviews during each stage
Poorly, because the executive should update the business case, not the PM
Poorly, because forecasts belong in the highlight report, not the case
A.why: Maintaining the business case means updating it at each stage end with progress data and the latest forecasts so the board can check justification (5.3.1).

whyNot.1: Benefits are mostly confirmed after closure; updating the case at a stage end is maintaining it.
whyNot.2: The PM prepares and maintains the business case on behalf of the executive.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports cover stage status; the business case holds the forecasts that justify continuing.

A.q: A candidate reads a question about Fernhollow and decides, from the scenario, that the action described is poor. Two options begin 'Poorly, because...'. One states a true fact from the manual that does not relate to the action; the other explains which rule the action breaks. What should the candidate do?
options: Choose the reason with more detail drawn from the manual
Choose the reason that explains the rule this action breaks
Reconsider the verdict, since both reasons are true statements
Choose the reason that mentions a fact from the scenario booklet
A.why: The right reason must be correct and must explain this situation; a true fact that does not explain the action is a distractor.

whyNot.0: Detail is not the test; a detailed true statement can still fail to explain the situation.
whyNot.2: Distractors are often true statements; that is no reason to doubt a well-founded verdict.
whyNot.3: Booklet facts can appear in any option; what matters is whether the reason explains the action.

B.q: One Fernhollow Kitchen recipe uses sesame, which has never been handled on site, so allergen controls are legally required. The board says that because the controls are compulsory, there is no need to justify which of the three control options is chosen. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
options: Well, because compulsory work is justified by the law that requires it
Well, because food safety risks are outside the board's risk appetite
Poorly, because the chosen option still needs justifying as best value
Poorly, because allergen controls are outside the project's scope
B.why: Even compulsory projects or requirements need justification of the chosen option as best value (2.1, 5.2.3).

whyNot.0: The requirement may be compulsory, but the choice between options must still be justified.
whyNot.1: True that the appetite for food safety risk is very low, but this does not remove the need to justify the option.
whyNot.3: Allergen controls are part of making the range, so they are within the project.

B.q: During initiation of the Fernhollow Kitchen launch, the project manager records 'a range of six plant-based ready meals in 400 Harbridge's stores' under the expected benefits heading of the business case. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because expected benefits are recorded in the business case
Yes, because a listing in 400 stores can be measured objectively
No, because benefits are recorded in the benefits management approach
No, because the range is an output, not a measurable improvement
B.why: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome; the range itself is an output (5.2).

whyNot.0: True that benefits go in the business case, but this entry is not a benefit.
whyNot.1: Being countable does not make an output a benefit.
whyNot.2: The benefits management approach sets out benefits reviews and actions; expected benefits are listed in the business case.

B.q: Greendale Ready Meals will co-manufacture two Fernhollow Kitchen recipes. It asks for a minimum volume of 150,000 meals so that its own investment in the work is worthwhile. Fernhollow's finance director says Greendale's reasons are not Fernhollow's concern. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
options: Well, because Fernhollow's executive owns the customer's business case
Well, because a supplier's costs are covered in its contract
Poorly, because each party needs its own justification to take part
Poorly, because the case should include the supplier's profit
B.why: All parties, including suppliers, need a balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify their involvement (2.1).

whyNot.0: True that the executive owns Fernhollow's business case, but this does not address the supplier's justification.
whyNot.1: The contract sets terms; it does not make the supplier's own justification irrelevant.
whyNot.3: The supplier has its own justification; its profit is not part of Fernhollow's business case.

C.q: In Fernhollow's trials stage, shelf-life tests show that two recipes last only six days. The project manager's exception report recommends launching four recipes. Before approving the exception plan, the board asks for the business case to be updated to show whether the four-recipe range is still worth doing. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the board checks the case when assessing an exception plan
Yes, because the senior user is accountable for the business case
No, because the business case is checked at planned stage boundaries
No, because four recipes meets the buyer's minimum, so no check is needed
C.why: The board checks continued justification at the end of each stage and when assessing an exception plan (5.3.1).

whyNot.1: The executive, not the senior user, is accountable for the business case.
whyNot.2: Planned stage ends are one check point, but the board also checks when assessing an exception plan.
whyNot.3: Meeting a buyer's minimum does not show the range is still desirable, viable and achievable.

C.q: In starting up the Fernhollow Kitchen launch, the project manager includes 'do nothing differently' as the first option in the outline business case, alongside a smaller and a full range launch. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because keeping the current position is what the board prefers
Yes, because it is the baseline for measuring the other options
No, because a mandate rules out keeping the current position
No, because options are assessed by the business layer beforehand
C.why: Do nothing differently comes first and is the baseline against which the benefits of the other options are quantified (5.3.1).

whyNot.0: Do nothing differently is included as a baseline, not because of any preference.
whyNot.2: A mandate starts the process; do nothing differently is still compared with the other options.
whyNot.3: Options are analysed as the business case is developed in the project.

C.q: Fernhollow's final stage covers the launch and the first eight weeks of sales. The project manager proposes keeping the project open for a further twelve months, after the range is handed to sales and operations, so the project can measure branded sales. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because benefits must be confirmed before a project can close
Yes, because the senior user is responsible for realizing benefits
No, because later benefits reviews are carried out by the business
No, because benefits are measured by the business layer in the final stage
C.why: The project plans post-project benefits reviews; the business carries them out after closure (5.3.1).

whyNot.0: Most benefits are confirmed after closure; the project does not wait for them.
whyNot.1: True that the senior user is responsible for realizing benefits after closure, but that does not justify keeping the project open.
whyNot.3: Post-project reviews happen after closure, not within the final stage.

reteach.title: Think like a referee: decision first, then the rule
reteach.question: A referee first decides foul or no foul, then names the rule. How does that help with 'and why?' questions?

blocks.body: Treat each question like a referee's call. First, the call: was the action right or wrong, given the facts? Then the citation: which rule makes it right or wrong? A referee who calls a foul but cites the offside rule is still wrong. In the exam, the right verdict with the wrong reason scores nothing.

items: Cover the options and say yes or no to yourself.
Uncover the two options with your verdict.
Ask of each: does this rule explain THIS action?

explain.h: Half the options go at once
explain.body: Two options share each verdict. Once you have decided the verdict from the facts, the other two options are out, whatever their reasons say.

test.q: A candidate reads a Fernhollow question with two 'Yes, because...' and two 'No, because...' options. From the facts, she is confident the action was appropriate. How many options can she rule out before comparing reasons?
options: Two, the options with the 'No' verdict
One, the weakest of the four reasons
Three, leaving the most detailed reason
None, as every reason must be compared
test.why: Deciding the verdict removes the two options with the other verdict, leaving two reasons to compare.

whyNot.1: The verdict removes two options at once, not one.
whyNot.2: Two options remain with her verdict; she must still compare their reasons.
whyNot.3: The opposite-verdict options can go without comparing their reasons.

explain.body: If the justification is no longer valid, the project should be stopped. Premature closure is decided by the project board, not the project manager.

test.q: Midway through Fernhollow Kitchen's development stage, Harbridge's withdraws the listing and no other buyer is interested. The board reviews the business case and decides to close the project early. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
options: Well, because the board closes the project when the PM requests it
Well, because a project no longer justified should be stopped
Poorly, because the listing fee has already been paid to the buyer
Poorly, because the PM should decide whether to close the project
test.why: Justification must remain valid throughout; when it is not, the project should be stopped (2.1).

whyNot.0: Here the board decided on its own review, and a PM request is not what makes stopping an unjustified project right.
whyNot.2: Money already spent does not justify continuing a project with no viable future.
whyNot.3: Premature closure is decided by the project board, not the project manager.

test.q: Fernhollow's project manager is checking the expected benefits listed in the Fernhollow Kitchen business case. Which entry is a benefit rather than an output or outcome?
options: Six recipes listed in 400 stores
Shoppers buying the brand each week
A recyclable tray and sleeve design
Branded sales of £6 million a year
test.why: A benefit is the measurable improvement from an outcome, such as a sales figure the business values.

whyNot.0: Products on shelf are outputs of the project.
whyNot.1: Changed shopper behaviour is an outcome.
whyNot.2: A pack design is an output.

explain.body: The permitted deviation in benefit targets before escalation, the benefits tolerance, is documented in the benefits management approach.

test.q: Fernhollow's board wants to record how far forecast branded sales may fall below target before the project manager must escalate. Where should this benefits tolerance be documented?
options: In the risk management approach
In the benefits management approach
In the project plan for the launch
In each stage's highlight report
test.why: Benefits tolerance is documented in the benefits management approach (5.2.2).

whyNot.0: The risk management approach holds risk procedures and scales, not benefits tolerance.
whyNot.2: The project plan sets the project's time and cost targets; benefits tolerance is recorded elsewhere.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports report stage status; they do not set tolerances.
